newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - JULY 10.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK FINANCIAL NEWS - JULY 10.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek financial press:

--After the news that inflation has stalled at 5.5 percent comes the news that the rate of revenues for the state from the general budget is still at 11.0 percent, despite earlier predictions that revenues were increasing by 17.0 percent. The latest news means there will be serious problems in meeting budget targets this year, demanding more efforts in 1998.

--More work is needed to push down inflation, according to the recent quarterly report by the Foundation of Economic and Industrial Research, IOVE. IOVE said that with the current mix of macro-economic policies being followed it would be difficult, if not impossible, for inflation to fall further by the end of the year.

--Accumulated debts by a number of public enterprises and utilies (DEKOs) will be able to be addressed by share capital increases involving either bonds or other lending products, in accordance with a new amendment voted through Parliament last week.

--The government is leaning towards reducing the amount employers pay in pension contributions for their employees, according to Labour and Social Security Minister MIltiades Papaioannou. The proposal is one of 10 promoted by the government and in line with Prime Minister Costas Simitis's vow to reduce to the minimal non-wage labour costs.

--Tuesday's Madrid summit agreement between Greece and Turkey was a much-needed shot in the arm for trading on the Athens Stock Exchange yesterday, with the general price index closing 1.82 percent up at 1,576.33 points.

--Procedures to list state-run Duty-Free Stores on the Athens Stock Exchange are being stepped up as part of the effort to raise inflow figures for the state. Yesterday's meeting between National Economy and Finance Minister Yiannos Papandoniou, Deputy Finance Minister George Drys and others decided that 25 percent of Duty-Free Stores should have been sold by the end of the year.

--The administration of the Agricultural Bank of Greece and representatives of Egnatia Bank will have their first meeting today on the purchase of the Bank of Central Greece by Egnatia, the sole bidder. ATE is hoping to bring Egnatia's offer of 7.3 billion drachmas up by 1.0-1.5 billion drachmas.

--Tax inflows for the months of May and June were at satisfactory high levels, Deputy Finance Minister George Drys told reporters yesterday, adding that surprise audits and tax checks by the ministry's financial crimes squad, SDOE, would continue and would focus on tourist enterprises in Attica and other regions.
--New Bank of Greece rules have raised the minimum level of equity and same capital needed for the establishment and operation of cooperative banks from 600 million drachmas to 1.2 billion drachmas.
--Greece plans to launch a Matador bond of around 25 billion pesetas (37.7 billion drachmas) with a seven-year maturity on the Spanish market.
